clue.text: Blamed Hood for having set weekly

indicators.note: to set something is to arrange it, so these letters are put into a new order

parts.note: the words as printed, but the parse needs an A where the second O stands: the setter's slip

explanation.surface: Robin Hood is blamed because he arranged something to happen every week.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is one letter out: BLAMED HOOD has a second O where the answer needs a second A, a slip in the clue as printed.
explanation.definitionFit: Hebdomadal is a formal word, from the Greek for a group of seven, meaning occurring once every seven days.

clue.text: A city girl?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the capital of South Australia
second meaning: a woman's first name

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a townie, a girl from the city; the question mark flags that the city and the girl share a name.
explanation.definitionFit: Adelaide is the capital of South Australia, named after Queen Adelaide, and is also a female first name.

clue.text: Some answer very difficult to turn aside?

indicators.note: some of the words means only a part of them, so the answer lies within the run of letters

parts.note: the run of letters inside these two words

explanation.surface: A question too tough to dodge: some answers are hard to sidestep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Difficult to' is just padding linking the hidden word to its definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To swerve is to veer suddenly to one side, which is to turn aside.

clue.text: Females in male quarters?

parts.note: he is the male pronoun
north and south, two of the four compass quarters

explanation.surface: It asks about women found in men's accommodation, such as a barracks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quarters' looks like lodgings but means compass points, N, S, E and W; here two of them follow the male pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: Hens are female birds, and the word is used for females generally, as in a hen party.

clue.text: Engineer talked of writer

indicators.note: something talked of is spoken, so what we need is a word that is heard like another

parts.note: Robert Louis Stevenson, the author of Treasure Island

explanation.surface: An engineer gossips about a novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: The writer and the engineer, George or Robert Stephenson of the Rocket locomotive, have names that are said the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: George Stephenson built early railways and the Rocket locomotive, making him a celebrated British engineer.

clue.text: Elementary protection?

parts.note: surface reading: basic, simple protection
setter's reading: protection against the elements, chiefly rain

explanation.walkthrough: 'Elementary' wants to mean basic; read it as 'of the elements', the weather, and it describes what you open in the rain.
explanation.definitionFit: A rain canopy carried over the head shelters you from wind and rain, the elements.

clue.text: Some say, superlatively fine friends, apparently

indicators.note: apparently says the answer only seems to describe something: read as an instruction, it tells you which way to read its first part

parts.note: pals are friends, and this word is the one that becomes pals when read from the bottom
the direction word in the answer, which is the instruction to read upwards

explanation.surface: People say some friends are the very best.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: read the answer as an instruction, SLAP written UP the column, and you get PALS, friends. 'Some say' marks the definition as colloquial.
explanation.definitionFit: Slap-up is informal for lavish or first-rate, as in a slap-up dinner, so it works as a superlative form of fine.

clue.text: Habit of refusal?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: custom, what one usually does
second meaning: the word of refusal, will not, contracted, which loses only its apostrophe

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a stubborn habit of saying no; the question mark admits the second half is the contraction with its apostrophe dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Wont is an old noun for a habit or custom, and the contraction won't is a refusal.

clue.text: We don't trouble about people having this sort of policy

indicators.note: to trouble something is to stir it up and disturb its order

parts.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
men are people

explanation.surface: Someone describes a heartless outlook: a policy of not bothering about other people.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of WE DONT go about MEN, and the whole lot is rearranged. 'This sort of policy' points to an insurance term.
explanation.definitionFit: An endowment policy is a kind of life insurance that pays a lump sum at maturity.

clue.text: Very often seen in bars

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the Italian for very

definitions.note: a description of the word rather than a synonym
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a direction that turns up in the bars of a musical score

explanation.surface: A regular drinker who is very often seen in bars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very' looks like an intensifier for 'often'; it is the definition, and the bars are bars of music, as in 'allegro molto'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian musical direction meaning very is used to strengthen tempo marks like allegro.

clue.text: Girl gets small sums, including gold

indicators.note: including means taking something in as a part, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: doles are small portions of money handed out
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: A young woman receives little payments, some of them in gold.
explanation.definitionFit: Dolores is a female first name, so it is an example of a girl.

clue.text: Animal breaks some wall?

indicators.note: breaking into something splits it open, so the intruder ends up in its middle

parts.note: part of something is some of it
an ape is an animal

explanation.surface: A creature smashes its way through a section of wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' reads as a quantifier for 'wall' but stands alone as PART, which the animal splits.
explanation.definitionFit: A parapet is a low protective wall along the edge of a roof, bridge or balcony.

clue.text: The state of the hair is sound

indicators.note: sound here means what is heard, so we want a word that is said the same way

parts.note: a mane is a long head of hair, said the same as the US state

explanation.surface: A hairdresser judges the condition of someone's hair to be healthy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The state of the hair' looks like one phrase about condition; it splits into 'The state' and 'the hair'.
explanation.definitionFit: Maine is a US state in New England.

clue.text: Danger to driver when carrying piles of scrap

indicators.note: one word carrying another holds it inside, as a bag carries its load

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: piles made into scrap are broken up, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A motorist is at risk when the truck ahead is loaded with heaps of scrap metal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piles of scrap' reads as a junk-heap load, but 'scrap' is a verb sense here: piles that are scrapped are broken up.
explanation.definitionFit: Wheelspin, where a tyre spins without gripping the road, is a hazard to a motorist, especially on wet or icy surfaces.

clue.text: School for shooting?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: ... College, an old English public school
second meaning: the American rifle maker and its repeating rifle

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a school that teaches marksmanship; the question mark flags two unrelated things sharing a name.
explanation.definitionFit: Winchester College is a famous English boarding school, and the Winchester is a well-known make of rifle.

clue.text: Is Ann Holt can contrive to appear cool

indicators.note: to contrive is to devise or rig up, so these letters are worked into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A question whether a woman called Ann Holt can manage to look unbothered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like the verb of the question but is part of the fodder too: ANN HOLT CAN supplies all ten letters, and 'contrive' rearranges them.
explanation.definitionFit: Being cool means calm and unruffled, which is what nonchalant means.

clue.text: It is Edna Strong's place to care for the wounded, possibly

definitions.text: place to care for the wounded

indicators.note: possibly suggests one of several arrangements, so the letters before it may be reordered

parts.note: every letter taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A sturdy woman called Edna runs a field hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: Edna Strong sounds like a nurse with a name; her whole introduction is the fodder, and 'possibly' at the end is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A dressing station is a first-aid post near a battlefield where injuries are bandaged before evacuation.

clue.text: Bird upset animals and fish

indicators.note: in a down entry, upset means turned upside down, so the word reads from the bottom up

parts.note: rats are animals
the ling is a fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: A bird has disturbed some animals and fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The starling is a common speckled songbird known for its huge swirling flocks.

clue.text: Bury man is given short break.

parts.note: to inter is to bury
Val, a man's name, short for Valentine

explanation.surface: A grim instruction: put a man in the ground, then take a quick rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bury' is not the Lancashire town but the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: An interval is a short pause, such as the break between the acts of a play.

clue.text: The naval manoeuvres include one big ship

indicators.note: to include something is to take it in, so a piece goes inside the others
manoeuvres are moves and shifts of position, so the letters are shifted around

parts.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A fleet's exercises feature a single enormous vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Naval manoeuvres' reads as a fleet exercise; 'manoeuvres' rearranges THE NAVAL with the numeral for one added.
explanation.definitionFit: A leviathan is a sea monster in the Bible, and by extension any huge thing, especially a very large ship.

clue.text: The prey of little boys?

parts.note: Vic is a short form of Victor, a boy's name
Tim is a short form of Timothy, another boy's name

explanation.surface: It asks what small boys hunt or tease.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little boys' are two short boys' names, Victor and Timothy cut down; the question mark flags that one phrase serves both.
explanation.definitionFit: A victim is one who suffers at the hands of another, the prey of a predator or bully.

clue.text: Walton's music?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: what an angler like Izaak Walton, author of The Compleat Angler, lands

definitions.note: a noun; 'music' stands for a piece of music
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a round for several voices, a kind of song

explanation.surface: It looks like a question about the composer William Walton's works.
explanation.walkthrough: The composer William Walton is the false trail; the Walton meant is Izaak Walton, the 17th-century writer on fishing.
explanation.definitionFit: A fisherman's haul is his catch, and a catch is also a comic round sung by several voices.

clue.text: Singer is drunk?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a songbird kept as a pet

definitions.note: a description: the answer is something that is drunk
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a sweet wine from the ... Islands, popular in Shakespeare's day

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as an accusation that a vocalist is intoxicated; 'drunk' is a verb, telling you the answer is also a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: The canary is a yellow songbird famed for singing, and canary is an old sweet wine from those islands.

clue.text: Stories about retiring old lawyer seen in Rugby

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps around another

parts.note: tales are stories

indicators.note: retiring means drawing back, so the word is read in the backward direction

parts.note: a King's Counsel; old in 1984 when a Queen reigned and lawyers were QCs

explanation.surface: Tales are told of a retired barrister who turns up at Rugby School.
explanation.walkthrough: Rugby is the school but also the game that took its name; the definition describes what you see in a rugby match.
explanation.definitionFit: Tackles, bringing down the ball carrier, are a constant sight in a game of rugby football.

clue.text: Objection arises over a player's property, perhaps

indicators.note: in a down entry, something that arises goes up, so it reads from the bottom

parts.note: a but is an objection, as in no ifs or buts
taken as written

explanation.surface: A protest is raised about who owns a footballer's or actor's belongings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Player' suggests sport or theatre; it is a musician, and 'perhaps' admits this is one example of an instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: A tuba is a large brass instrument, so it is an example of what a musician owns and plays.

clue.text: Girl isn't right about a single Shakespeare character

indicators.note: something that is not right is wrong or out of order, so its letters get reordered

parts.note: taken as written
a single is one

explanation.surface: A young woman is mistaken about one of Shakespeare's characters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Isn't right' reads as 'is wrong about', but it is the anagram signal for GIRL with ONE.
explanation.definitionFit: Goneril is King Lear's eldest daughter, one of the roles in Shakespeare's tragedy.

clue.text: Christie's heart is in this Biblical city

indicators.note: the heart of a thing is its middle, so only the centre is kept and the ends are dropped

parts.note: the first name of Agatha Christie, the crime novelist

explanation.surface: The core of a Christie mystery is set in a city from the Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: The surname is a pointer: you need her first name, Agatha, and its middle four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Gath was one of the five Philistine cities in the Old Testament, the home of Goliath.

clue.text: Lines written on one man or another

indicators.note: in an across entry, writing one thing on another puts it first with the other following straight after

parts.note: British Rail, the railway lines
Ian is a man's name

explanation.surface: Someone writes a short poem about a man, or perhaps a different man.
explanation.walkthrough: Lines are railway lines here, BR for British Rail, written on top of a man's name; 'another' then defines the result as a second man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Brian is also a man's first name, so it is another man after the one in the wordplay.

clue.text: Join the anti-reformers? Hosts of people do!

parts.note: a playful first half: to join is to go in, and those against reform want to keep things as they are
setter's reading: what a host does for guests, read as plural hosts

explanation.surface: A recruiting call to sign up with the conservatives, which crowds of people answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hosts of people' looks like 'crowds of people' but means people who are hosts. The first half seems to play on enter (join) followed by a sense of keeping, but it does not parse cleanly.
explanation.definitionFit: Hosts receive and amuse guests, which is what the verb meaning to show hospitality describes.
